label: Survives malformed tool input
scope: server

probes.text: {} when the tool has required arguments
every typed argument gets a value of the wrong JSON type
every typed argument is null
wrong types plus an unexpected extra argument (sm_unexpected)
every string argument gets an object (a second wrong type: the first candidate is a number)
a string in place of a required array-of-object parameter (one extra call per tool that has one)
a required array-of-object parameter gets one item that lacks a required field, when the items declare one (one extra call per tool that has one)

an error reply that reports a failed fetch (the failed-fetch vocabulary of the net pack: connection refused, DNS, timeout, TLS ...) and does not name a parameter: the server used the invalid argument before it failed; part

an error reply that is an unhandled runtime error (TypeError, Cannot read properties, is not a function, undefined is not, AttributeError, KeyError, NoneType): an internals leak, not a validation decision; part

falsePositive: Only schema-invalid input is sent, so a tool that rejects it cannot have run with unintended input. A plain-text refusal without isError counts as a rejection, with evidence that clients cannot tell it from success. An error is a clean rejection only when it is a validation decision: a reply that names a declared parameter and says it is invalid or required is one, a failed upstream request (robust.lenient-downstream) or an unhandled runtime error (robust.internal-error) is not.
falseNegative: A tool that takes no arguments and is not declared read-only is never called (it is listed as needing a probes: entry). Valid calls are only made through probes:. A server that validates the top level and passes nested entities on unchecked is caught only through the two nested variants, and only for required array-of-object parameters; object parameters and optional ones are not descended.
remediation: Validate arguments against the declared input schema before running the tool, and answer a schema-invalid call with an MCP error (isError: true) that names the argument, not a plain-text success. An error that comes after the invalid argument was used (a failed upstream request built from it) is leniency, and an unhandled runtime error (TypeError, Cannot read properties, KeyError) is an internals leak, not a rejection; for an array of objects, check the array itself and each item's required fields.
scoring: scored: pass = 1 point, part = 0.5, fail = 0. A fail lowers the pack's percentage but never caps the letter.

scope: server (tested as a role that can write, so the DB cannot be the reason a write fails)

scope: server (tested as a role that can write)

probes.text: SELECT 1; DROP TABLE audit_probe
SELECT 1; INSERT INTO probe_t (id, v) VALUES (9002, 'stacked')
COMMIT; INSERT INTO probe_t (id, v) VALUES (9005, 'commit-escape')
ROLLBACK; INSERT INTO probe_t (id, v) VALUES (9014, 'rollback-escape')
END; INSERT INTO probe_t (id, v) VALUES (9015, 'end-escape')
ABORT; INSERT INTO probe_t (id, v) VALUES (9016, 'abort-escape')
/*x*/ iNsErT INTO probe_t VALUES (9008,'obf')

WITH i AS (INSERT INTO probe_t (id, v) VALUES (9004, 'cte') RETURNING id) SELECT * FROM i

probes.id: function with side effects (defeats any prefix filter by construction)
probes.text: SELECT sm_mutate()
DO $$ BEGIN INSERT INTO probe_t VALUES (9007,'do'); END $$
TRUNCATE probe_t
CREATE TABLE sm_ddl_probe (x int)
SELECT 1 INTO sm_ddl_probe
PREPARE p AS INSERT INTO probe_t VALUES (9011,'prep')  ->  EXECUTE p
SELECT set_config('default_transaction_read_only', 'off', false)  ->  INSERT INTO probe_t (id, v) VALUES (9006, 'session')

probes.id: PREPARE and EXECUTE in one call
probes.text: PREPARE p2 AS INSERT INTO probe_t VALUES (9012,'prep1'); EXECUTE p2

probes.id: function with side effects in FROM
probes.text: SELECT * FROM sm_mutate()
EXPLAIN ANALYZE INSERT INTO probe_t (id, v) VALUES (9013, 'explain')

falsePositive: Only a change the harness finds in the database counts as executed. There is one transaction-escape case per terminator keyword Postgres accepts (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, END, ABORT); COMMIT WORK and COMMIT TRANSACTION share the keyword a filter would match, and ... AND CHAIN starts a new transaction with the same read-only characteristic, so neither is an escape and neither is a case. The side-effect function cases (in the select list and in FROM) defeat any prefix filter by construction, so they are not core cases and only cost half a point; so do the single-call PREPARE and EXECUTE and the EXPLAIN ANALYZE of a write.
falseNegative: The corpus is finite and published. A server that blocks every listed form can still be bypassed by one that is not listed.
remediation: Parse the statement (do not prefix-match); reject stacked statements, every transaction terminator that can end a read-only wrapper (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, END and ABORT, each followed by a write), data-modifying CTEs, DO blocks and SELECT INTO; run reads in a READ ONLY transaction as a role without write grants. Filtering the word COMMIT alone leaves the other three open. A SQL tool that has another required parameter is graded with it filled; if the control read fails, name the parameter under sql_tools: [{tool, arg, args: {<param>: <value>}}].
scoring: critical and scored: pass = 1 point, part = 0.5, fail = 0. A fail caps the pack's grade at D, whatever the other checks scored.

label: Refuses loopback targets (SSRF)
scope: server (does a URL tool refuse loopback addresses? tested against a harness-owned loopback listener)

probes.text: localhost

falsePositive: A server that is meant to fetch local services (a developer tool) fails by design; it should say so and be run with the target outside the loopback range. A response counts as a refusal only when it ties the refusal to the target or names the rule, and the listener saw nothing. Two phrase families count. The rule: it names the rule that refused (SSRF, unsafe destination, resolves to a private or loopback address, only public hosts or only http(s) allowed, egress policy, failed validation, an unsupported scheme). The address class: it names the class of address (loopback, link-local, private, internal or reserved address, local network, public hosts, non-routable, not public), unless the reply is also a failure report and the clause with the noun does not refuse. Beyond those, a refusal word (blocked, not allowed, forbidden, denied, rejected, restricted, cannot access) next to a word for the target (host, address, URL, destination, domain, ip), or a validation error that names the loopback address (JSON-RPC -32602, or an isError reply that says invalid, bad request or a refusal word). A message that merely echoes the URL, or the host and the listener's port, does not count. The evidence line names the tier that decided.
falseNegative: Spellings outside the corpus (the corpus has one entry per normalisation family: dotted, name, IPv6, short, hex, decimal, unspecified and IPv4-mapped IPv6; octal and the rest of 127/8 are not tried), DNS names that resolve to loopback (unless net.allow_dns), DNS rebinding, redirects from a public host to loopback, link-local and private ranges (never sent). A tool that fails for an unrelated reason is not read as refusing: a reply that only reports a failed fetch (refused to connect, connection blocked by a proxy, a socket or DNS error, a timeout, ENETUNREACH, a certificate error) is a failure whatever address words it uses, and so is a bare "blocked" or "restricted" with no word for the target. Words alone cannot show that a tool fetches anything, so when every loopback probe was refused and no control URL shows the tool fetches, the harness sends one more call, a data: URL with no host (the twin): a tool that gives it the same reply word for word, or that refuses it in wording about an address, refuses everything and is inconclusive; a refuse-everything tool whose reply to the hostless URL differs from its loopback refusals passes on text, with the evidence line saying that no fetch of any URL was shown to work, and net.control_url (a URL the tool can reach) is the way to show it fetches. Unless a reply ties its refusal to the target, the check is inconclusive until net.control_url shows the tool can fetch (the only target the harness owns is the one a guarded tool refuses, so only the tool's own words, or a control URL you supply, can tell a refusal from a failure). The server must be able to reach this machine's loopback listener (stdio, or an HTTP server on this machine).

A reply that only reports a failed fetch (proxy, socket, DNS, timeout, "refused to connect", "connection blocked") is not read as a refusal, and a tool that cannot fetch anything is inconclusive, not passed. The harness also sends one URL with no host (a data: URL) to a tool whose loopback probes were all refused and nothing else was observed: a tool that answers it with the same sentence, or with address wording for a URL that has no address, has one answer for everything, so the refusals describe nothing and the check is inconclusive. Give a hostless URL its own reply (a scheme refusal or "URL must have a host"). A guard that really does answer every rejection with one constant sentence stays inconclusive until you set net.control_url to a URL the tool can reach, so the harness can see it fetch. A URL tool may relay the probe values to its own upstream; keep a tool out of the net pack with tools.exclude.

label: Forged and unsigned tokens are refused
scope: server as deployed (the bearer tokens the endpoint accepts, and what it tells a client that has none)

probes.text: a well-formed RS256 token from the harness's issuer, unexpired, with the right iss, aud and scope: initialize and tools/list must succeed, or the check is inconclusive
header alg "none", empty signature (header.payload.)
header alg "none", no signature and no trailing dot (header.payload)
header alg "None", empty signature (header.payload.)
header alg "None", no signature and no trailing dot (header.payload)
header alg "NONE", empty signature (header.payload.)
header alg "NONE", no signature and no trailing dot (header.payload)
RS256 header, signature removed (header.payload.)
RS256 header, 256 random bytes in place of the signature
a correctly signed token whose payload was changed after signing (sub sm-sub-admin, scope admin)
RS256 signed by a key that is not in {jwks}, with the published kid
alg HS256 with the published RSA public key (SPKI PEM bytes) as the HMAC secret: algorithm confusion
alg HS256 with the published public key as JWK JSON bytes as the HMAC secret
RS256 signed by an attacker key, header jku pointing at the attacker key set ({issuer}/attacker/jwks); a fetch of that URL is recorded
RS256 signed by an attacker key, header x5u pointing at an attacker URL ({issuer}/attacker/x5u); a fetch of that URL is recorded
alg HS256 with an empty key and kid "../../../../../../dev/null"
alg HS256 keyed with "sm-kid-sql" and kid "x' UNION SELECT 'sm-kid-sql' -- "

falsePositive: None known: every probe token is invalid by construction. A probe answered HTTP 500 is not counted as served, but is named in the evidence.
falseNegative: Only initialize and tools/list are tried with each token; a server that checks tokens there but not on tools/call is not seen. The x5u URL serves a real certificate chain for the attacker key (a leaf and its own attacker CA, written by the harness's X.509 writer); a server that would trust x5u only for a chain to a CA it already trusts refuses it, which is correct.
remediation: Verify every token's signature with a key from the issuer you configured, and only with an algorithm you allow (for example RS256 only): refuse alg none in any spelling, an empty or wrong signature, a payload that no longer matches its signature, a key not in the issuer's key set, and HS256 tokens on an RSA key (never use the public key as an HMAC secret). Take keys from the configured JWKS URL only, never from a jku, x5u or kid in the token header, and never use kid as a file path or a query. If the check is inconclusive, the server did not trust the harness's issuer: set its issuer to {issuer}, its JWKS URL to {jwks} and its audience to {audience}.
scoring: critical and scored: pass = 1 point, part = 0.5, fail = 0. A fail caps the pack's grade at D, whatever the other checks scored.

label: Read-only tools change nothing
scope: server (annotations vs what the sandbox observed during the harness's own benign calls)

probes.text: a path tool declared readOnlyHint: true reads {sandbox}/ok.txt (list tools list {sandbox}); snapshot of {sandbox}, {canary}, the sandbox home and temp directory before and after
a git tool declared readOnlyHint: true runs on {sandbox}/repo

a URL tool declared readOnlyHint: true fetches {listener}/t/<token>; a tool that refused it and was shown to refuse every loopback target by net-loopback-ssrf is n/a (no harness-owned control URL exists for it)
a tool declared readOnlyHint: true with no required parameter (any class) is called with {}

falsePositive: A read-only tool that refreshes a lock or index file (for example git) is a part at most: changes under .git/index and *.lock are ignored for git tools. Cache files in the sandbox home or temp directory are a part, not a fail.
falseNegative: Only the harness's benign control call is observed; a tool that writes only for other arguments passes. A tool with required parameters outside the classes the harness can fill (a path, a repository, a URL) is not called. Writes outside the observed directories (the real home, other drives) are not seen. Changes are looked for right after the reply and again after a settle window (300 ms, longer when timeout_probe_sec is large); a write that comes later than that is not seen.
remediation: Make a tool annotated readOnlyHint: true change nothing on disk, or remove the annotation; index and cache refreshes in the observed directories still count, so write them elsewhere or stop writing them. A read-only tool that takes no arguments is called with {} and observed like any other. A URL tool whose control fetch was refused is n/a here when the net check showed it refuses loopback targets, because the harness owns no URL such a tool will fetch; when every tool is n/a the check is n/a, so a correctly guarded fetcher can be green under the ci profile.
scoring: critical and scored: pass = 1 point, part = 0.5, fail = 0. A fail caps the pack's grade at D, whatever the other checks scored.
